 Facilities As motorsports changes, Hendrick’s campus adapts
 Eight-figure investment reshapes race team’s headquarters with new facilities for training, manufacturing and corporate hospitality
 By Bret McCormick 10.30.2026 Share current article via %{socialType} Share current article via %{socialType} Share current article via %{socialType} Share current article via %{socialType} Share current article via %{socialType} Share current article via %{socialType} Share current article via %{socialType} Share current article via %{socialType} Hendrick Motorsports invested significantly in its campus during the last three years, as well as in the Ten Tenths Motor Club, a co-owned project with Speedway Motorsports. Hendrick Motorsports There are NASCAR corporate sponsor events. And then there is riding shotgun with Jeff Gordon as he whips a ZR1X Corvette around the turns and curves of Ten Tenths Motor Club. 
 That was the experience on offer during a Hendrick Motorsports event at the facility in fall 2025. The white-knuckled executives from Hendrick sponsors were relieved that Gordon’s Corvette came equipped with six-point safety belts and racing seats. It’s unlikely that the winding course and its 112 feet of elevation change helped their uneasy stomachs. 
 Gordon, who won 93 NASCAR Cup Series races and four Winston Cup Series titles during a Hall of Fame career driving the rainbow-patterned No. 24 car and now vice chairman of Hendrick Motorsports, holds the Ten Tenths course speed record, once hitting 130 miles per hour. 
 The facility — co-owned by Rick Hendrick and Speedway Motorsports, and plopped in the shadow of Charlotte Motor Speedway in Concord, N.C. — is built for event hosting. The 20,000-square-foot building and patio overlooking the course are useful assets in sponsor-driven motorsports. 
 Ten Tenths, which opened in October 2024, is a final puzzle piece tying together Hendrick’s hugely successful NASCAR teams and the automotive dealership businesses with its performance obsession. Gordon, never one to turn down a chance to rip a fast lap, gave more than 60 rides during the sponsor event last fall. 
 “Before Ten Tenths,” he said, “it was the one piece of our business that was missing — the actual getting behind the wheel.” 
 Hendrick’s valley 
 The rest of Hendrick’s real estate portfolio sits two miles away at the enterprise’s 300-acre main campus. Tucked into a small valley is the home of NASCAR’s winningest team, a handful of advanced manufacturing facilities, an elite athletic training center, a motorsports museum, the various offices of Hendrick’s businesses, several event hosting spaces and a massive car dealership. 
 When Hendrick bought the land in the early 1980s, it was just a mobile home at the end of a dirt road. In the last 3 1/2 years, the campus footprint expanded by 120 acres through an eight-figure investment by Hendrick and his partner, Gordon. 
 Shifts in the NASCAR world and the expansion of Hendrick’s businesses were primary sparks. The various facilities reflect a more professionalized NASCAR that, despite its mythical outlaw roots, is focused on competitive fairness. NASCAR’s 2022 introduction of the Generation 7 car prohibited teams from building their own car chassis, and NASCAR teams no longer paint their cars (they’re covered in decals instead). The space devoted to both endeavors pivoted to other uses. 
 Step inside Hendrick Motorsports and see what it takes to build a NASCAR powerhouse. From engineering and manufacturing to cutting-edge technology, the Charlotte-area campus is where ideas become speed and championship-winning cars take shape. 
 One such example: Where the chassis were once built, pit crew members are increasingly drawn from the stick-and-ball sports world and transformed into NASCAR tire changers and jack men. The training facility that Hendrick created and opened in January 2026 isn’t far off what the former college football players had when they were linebackers or cornerbacks. The athletic center houses an Atrium Health clinic for the pit crew and drivers’ conditioning and recovery, but it’s also open to any Hendrick employee free of charge. 
 “It comes from the heart, and that’s where Rick Hendrick is,” said Dr. Claude “T.” Moorman III, president of Atrium Health’s Musculoskeletal Institute. “But think about what a great business model it is. If you’re trying to recruit people to be on your race teams or drivers, or people to work in your shops, who wouldn’t want to be a part of that?” 
 Hendrick’s valley incorporates every aspect of his professional existence, whether building the largest privately held car dealership network in the U.S., or becoming NASCAR’s most successful team owner. Nods to the more than 300 NASCAR Cup Series wins and 15 championships pepper the site.
 In recent years, the campus’ critical mass of cutting-edge performance and manufacturing facilities has drawn GM Defense and Cadillac’s F1 team into its orbit. Instead of building chassis for racing stock cars, Hendrick is now building them for military vehicles. And their mechanical and manufacturing reputation attracted Cadillac F1 to build a 200,000-plus-square-foot, $150 million facility (leased from Hendrick) at the top of the hilly site for its new F1 program. 
 “A lot of people think of NASCAR as an old-school sport. And in some cases, it is because there is truly that history and that nostalgia that the fans love,” said Daniel Goldstein, Coca-Cola senior manager, sports marketing, who runs the brand’s NASCAR business. “But they’re not stuck in the past. When you walk into that complex, and then when you go to Ten Tenths, it goes toe to toe with any other professional sports facility that you go to.” 
 The collection of buildings and assets — everything that happens within them, and the investment and energy expended in them — reflects Hendrick and his sprawling enterprise. 
 “This will be a company that will continue to lead the pack from a technology side, the people, the culture, and then the facilities,” said Jeff Andrews, president and general manager of Hendrick Motorsports. “We get people from all around the world that come in here, from other racing series, from automotive manufacturers, that drive down in here and say, ‘I have never seen anything like this place in my life.’” 
 Ten Tenths 
 NASCAR has long been the American sport most comfortable with sponsors, and Hendrick has a variety of spaces available to its 30-plus team sponsors. Many are a year or two years old. Ten Tenths is the crown jewel.
 The size of the facility; the quality and premium aspect of the building and racecourse’s design; the night-lighting (which expands the number of hours people can drive); and the location (near a big city and two easily accessible airports) make the venue unique in the motorsports and performance car world. Other high-end driving locations and car clubs exist, but they’re often geographically isolated, and “then the whole luxury experience breaks down because it’s not seamless,” said Andy Thomas, Ten Tenths’ vice president of manufacturer relations. 
 There has been talk about turning Ten Tenths into a true club, creating an exclusive membership offering, but event hosting has proven so lucrative that there hasn’t been a major push toward that yet, Thomas said. 
 Speedway Motorsports operates the facility. It includes two kitchens and a chef overseen by Levy, and Hendrick Performance handles anything related to driving on the track. 
 The facility, with movable walls and an array of event layouts, has been kept purposely brand-agnostic, even though Hendrick Motorsports is a diehard General Motors- and Chevrolet-backed outfit. Agnosticism keeps Ten Tenths available to a wider array of automotive industry events and clients. 
 Gordon doesn’t drive corporate executives around the track at every event. But when he does, it’s a very different experience, one “you cannot replicate,” said Thomas. “You have to come here for it.”

(Hendrick Motorsports) On campus 
 In June, Gordon gave Atrium Health executives rides around Ten Tenths before they shifted to the main campus for a dinner event at the newly renovated Hendrick Team Center. 
 The team center formerly housed Gordon’s race team and the No. 24 DuPont car that helped establish Hendrick Motorsports as a NASCAR serial winner. The 325 Hendrick “H” logos on the far wall of the team center’s large main room — each representing a NASCAR win — allude to that foundation. Every hundredth “H” is red, and the “H” representing each of the organization’s 10 Daytona 500 victories is gold. 
 It’s much quieter in the team center than it used to be when company yoga or Bible studies are being held. The new acoustics are quite good, though, and the center hosts many of the more than 300 events occurring across the campus annually, ranging from a recent General Motors board meeting to private concerts. 
 The creation of more event spaces means more assets Hendrick Motorsports can provide to sponsors. “Hendrick Play Days” are part of Coca-Cola’s sponsorship contract, allowing the beverage giant to bring a group of people of its choosing once each year for behind-the-scenes tours of the campus, including of Hendrick’s private car collection, and driving experiences at Ten Tenths Motor Club. Hendrick’s campus helps Coca-Cola impress and reward its bottlers and best customers. 
 “These are not open to the public,” Goldstein said. “The access we’re afforded is what we like to call “only-Coke-can-do” moments. 
 Hendrick has three staff members managing its busy slate of events, including its own internal gatherings, which are held at the team center. The Hendrick workforce has grown to 500 people, and “we were running out of venues across greater Charlotte,” said Gene Cocchi, vice president of real estate for the Hendrick organization. 
 The team center is one of several repurposed campus buildings as the organization has grown and become more sophisticated since its founding in 1984. The recent spate of capital projects were renovations of existing building shells, except for the under-construction AVL Dyno building, where Hendrick race cars will be tested. 
 “Celebrating the past 40 years while building for the next 40 years,” said Roberto Medina, the recent facility overhaul’s project manager. 
 Next door to the team center sits the Atrium Health Motorsports Athletic Center. The museum at the front of the building is free to the public, and Hendrick Motorsports hosts a Fan Day around the October NASCAR race in Charlotte. 
 The 77-year-old Hendrick — “Mr. H,” as he’s called by his employees — has said he’ll never charge fans to come on his campus. And “campus” is the right word, because it feels in some ways like a university. 
 “We just have so many uses,” said Medina. “Some places are private, some open to the public and in between.” 
 The museum project started as a branding refresh with environmental design firms Forty Nine Degrees and Engin but quickly snowballed into a bigger effort, including higher ceilings, different car layouts, more interactive exhibits and a revamped team store. Some of the museum cars gleam as if they were just painted (or stickered). Others look like they did when they finished whichever famous race they won. The “Days of Thunder” movie car is a big draw right now.
 The cars used to be swapped out annually but are now rotated two or three times each year. Like many of the spaces on Hendrick’s campus, the museum is an ideal pre-function area. As Mr. H says: “The cars are the stars.” 
 Ten Tenths Motor Club, co-owned by Hendrick Motorsports and Speedway Motorsports, features a lighted road course and event facilities that provide driving experiences for sponsors and corporate clients. Hendrick Motorsports The last decimal point 
 Increasingly, the pit crew athletes are stars, too. 
 During the last 10 years, NASCAR team owners and pit crew chiefs realized that former college athletes’ physical skill sets couldn’t be taught, unlike changing a tire in 9 seconds. Recruitment and training efforts ramped up. New-age pit crews are generally less mechanically inclined than in the past, but more athletic; Kyle Larson’s 6-foot-2, 270-pound jackman, Eric Ludwig, can do a backflip. And they’re not all Caucasian, as was long the case. 
 Hendrick Motorsports has 51 pit crew members spread across its five Cup Series and O’Reilly Series teams, including seven developmental prospects who are transitioning into motorsports for the first time. 
 Hendrick’s pit crew roster gradually tripled in size, so the old athletic center was used in shifts. Room for the new one was created by NASCAR’s chassis manufacturing rule change. Redline Design Group, the lead architect on all the Hendrick projects, took Hendrick executives to Auburn and Clemson’s football practice facilities, Charlotte FC’s training ground and Fort Bragg. 
 The result makes clear NASCAR’s greater emphasis on pit stops. 
 There is a high-tech and spacious weight room laden with biometric sensors but also a climbing wall, key for pit crew members who need vice grips. 
 The Charlotte FC people suggested a kombucha kegerator, which quickly became a favorite of Evan Kureczka, Hendrick Motorsports athletic director, who oversees the pit crews’ training and performances. There is a barber shop, film rooms, meeting space, all the latest hydrotherapy and sauna offerings, red light therapy and a locker room, fitted out by Longhorn Lockers, that wouldn’t be out of place in FBS college football. 
 NASCAR has one of the longest seasons in pro sports, so recovery is a key emphasis in the athletic center and the appended Atrium Health clinic. 
 “If you look at any of the NFL programs, or even the high-level collegiate teams, and you walk into their performance center, you’ll see doctors there, you’ll see athletic trainers, nutritionists, sports psychologists … you’ll see every animal in the Ark,” said Atrium Health’s Moorman, who was formerly the Baltimore Ravens’ team doctor and worked closely for years with Duke basketball. “What’s unique about the Hendrick facility is this is the first time it’s been done in NASCAR. But we drew from all those other experiences in putting it together.” 
 Hendrick pit-stop times have steadily improved as the 2026 Cup Series season approaches its conclusion; normally, the opposite happens as crews wear down. 
 “If you want to see a guy who’s a techno geek, that’s Jeff Gordon,” said Moorman. “He really drills down to the last decimal point on everything for performance. That’s reflected in how they do things.” 
 Rick Hendrick's campus began in the 1980s as a mobile home at the end of a dirt road, progressing over the decades into a 300-acre collection of elite automotive, athletic, and manufacturing spaces. Hendrick Motorsports Gordon said the pit crew made the difference in Larson’s Kansas victory the day before. Larson’s crew ranked among the top five of 36 teams in most key pit-stop metrics, helping him secure his second Cup Series victory of the season. The win extended Larson’s lead in the championship standings to 26 points over Denny Hamlin with six races remaining in the Chase.
 “Kyle drove a great race. Everything was executed,” Gordon said. “But if you watch the race, I mean, we’re talking about tenths of a second between the top teams of whether or not you’re coming off pit road first or third or fourth.” 
 It felt like another justification for Hendrick’s overall capital projects effort, the investment proving worthy. Even the kombucha kegerator. 
 “Athletes are healthier and happier and more engaged and just feel like a bigger part of the organization than they ever have because of that facility,” Gordon said. “You can’t quantify that.”
